principle: Reduce exposure by targeting known sources and measured contamination first. Prefer actions with low downside, clear exposure logic, and authoritative support; avoid implying that eliminating one product prevents disease.

tiers.label: Well-supported action
tiers.definition: A practical step with a clear exposure pathway and support from authoritative guidance or established exposure science.

tiers.label: Reasonable precaution
tiers.definition: A low-burden step that may reduce exposure, but the size of the benefit is uncertain or highly context-dependent.

tiers.label: Uncertain / avoid overclaiming
tiers.definition: A claim or consumer practice where evidence is too weak, product-specific, or indirect to present as a reliable health-protection measure.

categories.title: Drinking water
categories.summary: Start with measurement. Water treatment choices should follow the contaminant actually present, its concentration, and validated treatment performance.

actions.action: Use local water-quality reports or laboratory testing when contamination is a realistic concern.
actions.rationale: Testing converts a vague concern into a specific contaminant-and-concentration question.
actions.limitation: A test result still needs interpretation against an applicable regulatory or health-based benchmark.

actions.action: If a contaminant is confirmed, choose treatment certified for that specific contaminant and maintain it as directed.
actions.rationale: Treatment performance depends on technology, certification, installation, and replacement schedule.
actions.limitation: No single filter removes every contaminant, and poorly maintained systems can underperform.

actions.action: Use an alternative drinking-water source temporarily when authorities issue a contaminant-specific advisory.
actions.rationale: This can reduce ingestion while testing, remediation, or treatment decisions are underway.
actions.limitation: The value depends on the contaminant and advisory; bottled water is not automatically contaminant-free.

categories.title: Food & food contact
categories.summary: Food exposure can come from residues, environmental contamination, processing, or food-contact materials. Focus on identifiable sources rather than broad food fear.

actions.action: Follow official food recalls and contaminant advisories when a specific product or source is identified.
actions.rationale: Targeted advisories address a known exposure source rather than an assumed one.
actions.limitation: General avoidance beyond the affected product or source may not meaningfully reduce exposure.
actions.source_label: FDA — Recalls, Market Withdrawals, & Safety Alerts

actions.action: Avoid repeatedly heating food in worn or damaged food-contact materials when the material is not intended for that use.
actions.rationale: Heat, wear, food chemistry, and contact time can influence migration from some materials.
actions.limitation: The actual exposure depends on the specific polymer, additive, coating, temperature, and food.

actions.action: Do not assume that 'chemical-free,' 'natural,' or 'BPA-free' means a product has no endocrine-active chemistry.
actions.rationale: Substitution can change the chemical without establishing lower exposure or lower hazard.
actions.limitation: A substitute may be safer, equivalent, or less studied; the label alone does not answer that question.

categories.title: Cookware
categories.summary: Cookware decisions should be based on material, condition, intended use, and temperature—not broad labels such as 'nonstick equals toxic.'

actions.action: Use cookware according to manufacturer temperature and care instructions.
actions.rationale: Material performance and degradation depend strongly on use conditions.
actions.limitation: This is a materials-exposure precaution, not evidence that normal use of a specific product causes endocrine harm.

actions.action: Replace cookware with severely damaged, peeling, or degraded food-contact surfaces.
actions.rationale: Physical deterioration can change food contact and migration behavior.
actions.limitation: Damage does not identify which chemical, if any, is being transferred at a meaningful dose.

actions.action: Avoid claims that one cookware material is universally 'toxin-free' or medically superior.
actions.rationale: Every material has its own exposure profile, use conditions, and tradeoffs.
actions.limitation: Comparisons require compound-specific migration and exposure data.

categories.title: Plastics
categories.summary: Plastic is a materials category, not one chemical. Reduce unnecessary migration opportunities when practical, while avoiding unsupported blanket claims.

actions.action: For hot food or liquids, use containers intended for the temperature and application.
actions.rationale: Heat can increase migration for some polymers or additives.
actions.limitation: The magnitude and relevance depend on the exact material and chemical.

actions.action: Retire heavily worn food-storage plastics when replacement is easy.
actions.rationale: Aging, abrasion, and repeated heating can alter material surfaces and migration behavior.
actions.limitation: This does not mean that visible wear equals a harmful endocrine dose.

actions.action: Do not use recycling codes alone as a health-risk score.
actions.rationale: A recycling code identifies a resin category, not the full additive package, dose, or endocrine activity.
actions.limitation: Risk interpretation requires more information than the code.

categories.title: Cosmetics & personal care
categories.summary: Ingredient identity and frequency of use matter more than broad claims about an entire product category.

actions.action: Read ingredient labels when trying to avoid a specific known ingredient.
actions.rationale: Ingredient-based avoidance is more precise than avoiding an entire category without knowing the formulation.
actions.limitation: Some fragrance ingredients may be grouped under permitted labeling conventions, and formulas can change.

actions.action: Reduce unnecessary use of multiple fragranced products if fragrance-related exposure is a concern.
actions.rationale: Using fewer products can reduce aggregate exposure to some formulation ingredients.
actions.limitation: The size of any endocrine-related benefit is uncertain and ingredient-specific.

actions.action: Do not treat 'clean beauty' or 'natural' marketing as an evidence grade.
actions.rationale: Marketing terms do not substitute for ingredient identity, exposure measurement, or toxicology.
actions.limitation: Individual products still require ingredient-specific evaluation.

categories.title: Household dust & indoor environment
categories.summary: Indoor dust can carry semi-volatile chemicals released from products and building materials. Source control and routine cleaning can reduce dust contact without implying disease prevention.

actions.action: Wash hands before eating, especially for children with frequent hand-to-mouth contact.
actions.rationale: Hand washing reduces ingestion of dust and residues carried on hands.
actions.limitation: It reduces one exposure route and does not eliminate airborne or dietary sources.

actions.action: Use routine dust control such as damp dusting and effective vacuuming.
actions.rationale: Lower dust loading can reduce contact with chemicals that partition into indoor dust.
actions.limitation: The actual reduction in a specific endocrine-active chemical depends on the source and room conditions.

actions.action: For confirmed PCB-containing building materials, follow professional and regulatory remediation guidance.
actions.rationale: PCBs in older materials are a source-specific contamination problem requiring controlled management.
actions.limitation: Do not disturb suspect materials solely on the basis of building age; identification and proper handling matter.
actions.source_label: U.S. EPA — PCBs in Building Materials

categories.title: Clothing & textiles
categories.summary: Textile treatments vary widely. Product disclosure and actual chemistry matter more than broad assumptions about all clothing.

actions.action: When buying new products, prefer items with clear disclosure if avoiding a specific treatment such as intentionally added PFAS.
actions.rationale: Disclosure makes source avoidance more targeted and verifiable.
actions.limitation: A marketing claim may not describe every component or legacy contamination source.

actions.action: Avoid replacing functional clothing solely because of a vague chemical concern unless the product chemistry is known.
actions.rationale: Replacement can create cost and waste without demonstrating meaningful exposure reduction.
actions.limitation: A confirmed contaminated or recalled product is a different situation.

actions.action: Do not infer internal dose from direct skin contact alone.
actions.rationale: Dermal absorption varies by chemical, formulation, skin contact, duration, and physicochemical properties.
actions.limitation: Some compounds can be absorbed dermally; the point is that contact and absorbed dose are not equivalent.
